The King of the Monsters is back — bigger, bloodier, and, for the first time ever, rated R. Godzilla Minus Zero opens in theaters across North America on Friday, November 6, and forecasters say the kaiju could stomp its way to the top of the weekend box office.

The film, distributed in North America by GKIDS, opened in Japan on Tuesday, November 3 — Godzilla Day, the anniversary of the original 1954 film — after a one-night IMAX early-access event. It is the sequel to 2023's Godzilla Minus One, which became a worldwide phenomenon and won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects.

Director Takashi Yamazaki returns as writer, director, and visual effects supervisor. With that Oscar win, he became only the second director since Stanley Kubrick to take home the visual effects award, and Minus One became the only Godzilla film in 70 years to win an Oscar — and the highest-grossing live-action Japanese film ever in North America, finishing with $57 million domestically after an $11.4 million U.S. opening.

This time, the Motion Picture Association rated the film R for "some violent content/bloody images" — the first R rating in the franchise's history. Minus One carried a PG-13. The sequel runs 135 minutes, ten minutes longer than its predecessor.

The story picks up in 1949, two years after the events of Minus One, and continues the story of the Shikishima family, with Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe, and Sae Nagatani all returning. A second kaiju joins the fight — The Hollywood Reporter's review out of the New York Film Festival identifies the three-headed King Ghidorah as the new threat.

The film is also a technical milestone: it is the first Japanese production ever shot for IMAX, with 75 minutes presented in the expanded 1.90:1 aspect ratio. It currently holds a Metascore of 75, and its festival premieres this fall drew rapturous reactions.

Box Office Pro projects a $25 million to $35 million opening weekend in North America, and Deadline's preview puts the worldwide opening near $60 million. One forecaster has Godzilla edging out Warner Bros.' animated The Cat in the Hat — projected around $30.5 million — for the weekend crown, a prize no Toho-made Godzilla film has ever taken in North America. Even a mid-$20 million debut would be the biggest opening ever for GKIDS, beating the $13 million debut of The Boy and the Heron in 2023.

The rest of the weekend field sits well behind. Sony's Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, the Indian epic that opened today, is projected at $6 million to $10 million over four days from about 1,300 theaters. Searchlight's Wild Horse Nine, Martin McDonagh's first film since The Banshees of Inisherin, is tracking near $7 million from about 1,000 locations. The kaiju's India release, meanwhile, was pushed to November 20 to clear Ramayana's two-week IMAX exclusivity there.

Yamazaki told IGN he had to set aside the urge to outdo the Oscar-winning original, saying that trying to top it for awards or scale was the wrong motivation. "He made it to have fun," as one report put it — and early reviews suggest the fun is landing.

Analysis: Why this opening matters beyond the monster

Minus One proved a subtitled Japanese film with a modest budget could become a global event and win an Oscar. Minus Zero is the test of whether that was lightning in a bottle or the start of something durable. An R rating, a bigger budget, a second monster, and the first-ever Filmed for IMAX Japanese production all raise the stakes — and the opening-weekend race against a family cartoon will tell Hollywood how far the kaiju's American audience has grown. If Godzilla takes the crown, it will be the first time a Toho-made Godzilla film has ever won a North American weekend, and a signal that the biggest monster in movie history finally has a mainstream American audience to match.
